interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on sketching a parabola from its rule. The main picture is a parabola, a sketch drawn from its rule y = ax² + bx + c, with handles for a, b and c. Three clues light up on it as markers: the point (0, c) where it crosses the y-axis, the roots where it crosses the x-axis, and the turning point halfway between them. Beside it a small table gives y for whole-number x, with the step from each y to the next written between them. The markers light up one at a time over the first screens. Screens: 1 opens on y = x² − 2x − 8 with only the a handle and lets you drag a from 1 to −1 (the handle skips 0, where the rule has no x² and its graph is a straight line), which flips the U to an upside-down U, because far from 0 the ax² part outgrows the rest (the other markers wait for screens 3 and 5); 2 asks whether y = 3 + 2x − x² has a highest or a lowest point; 3 lights (0, c): at x = 0 the x² and x parts are 0, so y = c, here (0, −8); 4 asks where y = (x − 3)(x + 2) crosses the y-axis; 5 writes the rule three ways, x² − 2x − 8 = (x − 4)(x + 2) = (x − 1)² − 9, each giving one clue, lights the roots −2 and 4 from the second, and the turning point halfway, at x = 1, because the curve is the same either side of its line of symmetry, height 1 − 2 − 8 = −9, opening on a closer view that widens once you move a handle, then frees all three handles so you can watch the markers move with the curve; 6 is a spot-the-slip: a working that finds the roots of x² − 6x + 5 first, by setting it to 0, then calls a root, (1, 0), the turning point, and you pick the line that slipped; 7 shows the table for y = x² − 2x − 8 from x = −2 to 4, y = 0, −5, −8, −9, −8, −5, 0, with steps −5, −3, −1, 1, 3, 5, each 2 more than the last, which is 2a, with the reason below, and a second table for y = 2x² − 2x − 8 whose steps −8, −4, 0, 4, 8, 12 are each 4 more, 2a with a = 2; 8 gives the table 3, 6, 13, 24, 39 and asks for a; 9 lays the line y = mx + c across y = x², with handles for the line's slope m and the line's c, where the line crosses the y-axis, as in Straight-line graphs (the same letter does the same job as the curve's c), opening on y = x + 2, which crosses at (−1, 1) and (2, 4), and a readout of the crossings as two, one or none; 10 asks how many times y = 2x − 1 meets y = x²; 11 asks which sketch is y = 2x² − 8x + 6; 12 asks whether y = x² + 4x + 7 crosses the x-axis; 13 asks where y = 2x − 8 meets y = x² − 2x − 8. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to pick one answer from three. A wrong pick puts its numbers back into the rule and shows they do not fit. The steps in the table change by 2a because, from x to x + 1, ax² grows by a(2x + 1), which is 2a more each time x goes up by 1, while bx grows by b every time and c not at all. The crossings readout comes from setting x² = mx + c, which is x² − mx − c = 0, where a = 1, b = −m and the plain number is −c, so b² − 4ac = m² − 4 × 1 × (−c) = m² + 4c, with the line's m and c: positive, two crossings; 0, one; negative, none.
interactive.ignores: The curve is drawn only over the stretch of x on screen; it carries on rising or falling either side. The handles move in whole steps so the markers land on readable numbers; any values work. The table shows whole-number x only; the curve runs smoothly between them. Roots that are not whole are shown to two decimal places. When the rule has no real roots the picture shows no x-crossings; it has two complex roots then, numbers off the number line, for the Complex numbers course. On the line screens the curve is y = x² only, to keep the counting plain.

explain.text:
A quadratic's graph is a parabola, a U-shaped curve,[^1] and three clues in its rule y = ax² + bx + c sketch it before you plot a single point. The sign of a says which way up it opens. c says where it crosses the y-axis. The roots, when it has them, say where it crosses the x-axis, and the turning point sits halfway between them.

Each clue comes straight from the rule. Far enough from 0, either way, x² is a big positive number that outgrows bx and c: at x = 100, x² − 2x − 8 is 10,000 − 200 − 8, and at x = −100 it is 10,000 + 200 − 8. So out at the ends y takes the sign of a. If a is positive the parabola opens upward,[^2] a U with a lowest point; if a is negative both ends fall, and it is an upside-down U with a highest point. At x = 0, ax² and bx are both 0, which leaves y = c, so the curve crosses the y-axis at (0, c).[^3] On the x-axis y is 0, so the crossings are the solutions of ax² + bx + c = 0, the roots from lesson 3 or the formula in lesson 5. The line of symmetry from lesson 4 runs through the turning point, and the curve is the same either side of it, so a height of 0 on one side is matched by a height of 0 the same distance the other side: an upside-down U's highest point sits in the middle of its roots,[^4] and a U's lowest point does too. Take y = x² − 2x − 8 = (x − 4)(x + 2). a is 1, so it is a U. It crosses the y-axis at (0, −8) and the x-axis at −2 and 4. Halfway is x = 1, and there y = 1 − 2 − 8 = −9, so the turning point is (1, −9), just what the completed-square form (x − 1)² − 9 gives.[^5] Setting y to 0 finds the roots, not the turning point: x² − 2x − 8 = 0 gives −2 and 4, where the height is 0, while the lowest point is at −9.

a is not a slope, though it sits where m sits in y = mx + c. A straight line climbs by the same step each time x goes up by 1, and that step is m. Read a as a slope and y = x² − 2x − 8 should climb by 1 each step. From x = −2 to 4 it goes 0, −5, −8, −9, −8, −5, 0: it falls by 5, 3 and 1, then climbs by 1, 3 and 5. Each step is 2 more than the last, and that 2 is 2a. From x to x + 1, ax² grows by a(2x + 1), which is 2a more each time; bx grows by b every time and c not at all. So a sets how fast the steps change, which is how sharply the curve bends: the further a is from 0, the narrower the U. Because the steps change every time, the curve bends all the way along, with a rounded bottom, not a point or straight sides.

The same reading shows where a straight line meets the curve. Where they meet, both rules give the same y, so set them equal. For y = x² and y = x + 2, x² = x + 2, so x² − x − 2 = 0, which is (x − 2)(x + 1) = 0: they meet at (2, 4) and (−1, 1). Its discriminant counts the crossings before you solve, because two distinct real roots, one repeated root or no real roots[^6] mean the line crosses twice, touches once or misses. y = 2x − 1 gives x² − 2x + 1 = 0, with b² − 4ac = 4 − 4 = 0, so it touches at (1, 1); y = x − 1 gives x² − x + 1 = 0, with 1 − 4 = −3, so it misses. **a's sign gives which way up, (0, c) the y-crossing, any roots the x-crossings, and the turning point sits halfway between them.**

analogy.text: Remember twice the current, four times the heat? P = I²R is a parabola with a = R, b = 0 and c = 0. R is positive, so it is a U: the heat rises whichever way the current flows. It passes through (0, 0), its one repeated root is 0 A, and its lowest point sits there. Through a 2 Ω resistor it gives 0, 2, 8, 18 and 32 W at 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 A, and the steps 2, 6, 10 and 14 W grow by 4, which is 2 × R, just as a parabola's steps grow by 2a.
analogy.breaks: A resistor's R is positive, so this curve never turns upside down, while a can be negative. And with no b or c its turning point is fixed at (0, 0), where a general quadratic's moves as b and c change.

practice.text:
- Read a, wherever it sits in the rule: positive gives a U with a lowest point, negative an upside-down U with a highest point.
- Put x = 0: the curve crosses the y-axis at (0, c).
- Find the roots: factorise if a pair comes quickly (lesson 3), else use the formula (lesson 5). Work out b² − 4ac first; negative means it never crosses the x-axis.
- Find the turning point: halfway between the roots, or at x = −b ÷ 2a, which works with no roots too. Put that x back into the rule for its height.
- Mark the points and draw one smooth curve through them, the same either side of the line of symmetry, rounded at the turning point.
- For a line meeting the curve, set the two rules equal, take everything to one side, and use b² − 4ac to count the crossings before you solve. Put each x into the line to get its y.

**Rule of thumb:** The turning point's x is the average of the two roots. Check a sketch by trying one more x in the rule and seeing that the point sits on your curve.

**Worked example:** Sketch y = −x² + 2x + 8. a is −1, so an upside-down U. At x = 0 it is 8, so it crosses the y-axis at (0, 8). It is −(x² − 2x − 8) = −(x − 4)(x + 2), so the roots are −2 and 4. Halfway is x = 1, and y = −1 + 2 + 8 = 9, so the highest point is (1, 9). Where does the line y = x + 2 meet it? −x² + 2x + 8 = x + 2, so x² − x − 6 = 0, with b² − 4ac = 1 + 24 = 25, so two crossings. (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 3 or −2, and the line gives the points (3, 5) and (−2, 0). Check x = 3 in the curve: −9 + 6 + 8 = 5.

**Common mistakes**
- Reading a as the slope. In 2x² + x + 3 the steps go 3, 7, 11, 15: they grow by 4, which is 2a, so a = 2, not 3.
- Setting y = 0 to find the turning point. That gives the roots: x² − 6x + 5 has roots 1 and 5, and its turning point is halfway, (3, −4).
- Taking the first term as a. In 3 + 2x − x², a is −1, so it has a highest point.
- Drawing the bottom as a point, or the sides as straight lines. The steps change every time, so the curve bends all along.
- Setting y = 0 to find where a line meets the curve. Set the two rules equal instead.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the U flipping as a changes sign, the y-crossing (0, c) following c, and the turning point staying halfway between the roots, when you drag the handles for a, b and c.

checks.label: The graph of a quadratic function is a U-shaped curve called a parabola: on every screen and every setting tried on the handles, the curve drawn is the rule's own and is the same either side of its turning point, at x = −b ÷ 2a

The graph of y = ax² + bx + c crosses the y-axis at the point (0, c): on every screen that marks it, and at every a, b and c tried on the handles, the square sits at (0, c) labelled with that c; on the line screens the line's square sits at its own c

If the sign of the leading coefficient a is positive (a > 0), the parabola opens upward: at every a tried on the handles the rule at x = 100 and x = −100 takes the sign of a, the picture says both ends rise for a > 0 and fall for a < 0, and every turning point drawn is a lowest point for a > 0 and a highest point for a < 0

A parabola's maximum height sits in the middle of its roots, and a U's lowest point does too: on every screen and at every a, b and c tried on the handles, the turning point drawn is at x = −b ÷ 2a, on the dashed line of symmetry, at the rule's own height there, and halfway between the two roots drawn

The discriminant distinguishes two distinct real roots, one repeated real root, or non-real complex roots only: at every a, b and c tried on the handles the picture draws two, one or no roots as b² − 4ac is above, at or below 0; on the line screen x² = mx + c becomes x² − mx − c = 0, whose b² − 4ac is m² + 4c, and at every m and c tried the crossings drawn are two, one or none to match, each on both the curve and the line, with the readout saying which

Each table's steps are the differences of neighbouring heights and grow by 2a every time: x² − 2x − 8 gives 0, −5, −8, −9, −8, −5, 0 with steps −5, −3, −1, 1, 3, 5, each 2 more (a = 1); 2x² + x + 3 gives 3, 6, 13, 24, 39 with steps 3, 7, 11, 15, each 4 more, so a = 2; and at every a, b and c tried, from x to x + 1 the rule grows by a(2x + 1) + b
Every puzzle accepts only its right answer, worked out from its own rule, and each wrong pick put back into the rule does not fit, with the hint quoting the rule's own numbers

The worked numbers: 10,000 − 200 − 8 at x = 100; −2 and 4 with the turning point (1, −9) from 1 − 2 − 8; (0, −8); (0 − 3)(0 + 2) = −6; 1, 5 and (3, −4) from 9 − 18 + 5; the tables; y = x + 2 meeting y = x² at (−1, 1) and (2, 4) with 1 + 8 = 9; 4 − 4 = 0 touching at (1, 1); 1 − 4 = −3; 16 + 16 = 32 and 0 − 16 = −16; 2 + 8 + 6 = 16 and 8 − 16 + 6 = −2; 16 − 28 = −12 and (x + 2)² + 3; (0, −8) and (4, 0) with 2 × (−2) − 8 = −12; and the screens' words quote the same numbers

Before Check a puzzle shows only its question: its curve or line, turning point, crossings and the change in the steps stay hidden; after a right answer they arrive, and a wrong pick puts its own numbers back into the rule, in red
Every label on the pictures finds a clear spot, inside its graph and off the other labels and the markers, on every screen and at every setting tried on the handles
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s
